Sec. 1.
1

This first section of the 14 November 1842 Nauvoo habeas corpus ordinance was one of the most heavily edited portions of the entire ordinance. Nauvoo’s leadership seems to have vacillated over who was authorized to issue writs of habeas corpus under the ordinance. Section 1 of the 1827 Illinois statute on habeas corpus, upon which Nauvoo’s ordinance was based, limited the right to issue writs of habeas corpus to the state supreme court or the county circuit courts during their respective terms or to any of those courts’ judges individually during the courts’ vacations. Accordingly, early drafts of the city ordinance granted the power to the municipal court or any of its justices. However, perhaps recognizing the difficulty of appealing directly to the judges of the supreme and circuit courts, in 1835 the Illinois state legislature passed an act requiring the circuit court justices to appoint a master in chancery for each county who would then be authorized to issue certain procedural writs, such as those of habeas corpus. The final version of the Nauvoo ordinance similarly shifted the responsibility for issuing writs of habeas corpus from the justices to the clerk of the municipal court. (An Act Regulating the Proceeding on Writs of Habeas Corpus [22 Jan. 1827], Public and General Statute Laws of the State of Illinois, pp. 322–323, sec. 1; An Act to Provide for Issuing Writs of Ne Exeat and Habeas Corpus, and for Other Purposes [11 Feb. 1835], Public and General Statute Laws of the State of Illinois, p. 145, secs. 1–2.)

In habeas corpus proceedings, courts only had the authority to remand prisoners and set their bail or to discharge them from custody. An editorial in the 15 August 1842 issue of the Times and Seasons acknowledged that habeas corpus hearings could not determine innocence or guilt, demonstrating that at least some church leaders were aware of the limitations of habeas corpus. Nevertheless, on at least two occasions the Nauvoo Municipal Court acquitted the prisoners from all charges in addition to discharging them from custody. (Tucker, Blackstone’s Commentaries, 1:291–292; Kent, Commentaries on American Law, 2:25; “Persecution,” Times and Seasons, 15 Aug. 1842, 3:888–889; Nauvoo Municipal Court Docket Book, 17–19 [second numbering], 51–52.)

As the city council deliberated over the ordinance, Sloan, both unidentified scribes, and, in a few instances, JS made changes to this copy of the ordinance. Most of these changes were minor, such as spelling corrections, though other small changes appear to have been made to increase the inclusivity of the ordinance by adding plural nouns or variant pronouns. For example, “or prisoners” was routinely added after “prisoner” and “his or her” was universally changed to “his, her, or their.” Once the council completed its deliberations and passed the ordinance on 14 November 1842, JS signed this rough copy. Sloan later copied the ordinance into the Nauvoo City Council minute book, and in accordance with the law, a copy was also published in a newspaper, the Wasp, on 3 December 1842.

footnotes.text: In habeas corpus proceedings, courts only had the authority to remand prisoners and set their bail or to discharge them from custody. An editorial in the 15 August 1842 issue of the Times and Seasons acknowledged that habeas corpus hearings could not determine innocence or guilt, demonstrating that at least some church leaders were aware of the limitations of habeas corpus. Nevertheless, on at least two occasions the Nauvoo Municipal Court acquitted the prisoners from all charges in addition to discharging them from custody. footnotes.text: James Sloan handwriting begins.

This first section of the 14 November 1842 Nauvoo habeas corpus ordinance was one of the most heavily edited portions of the entire ordinance. Nauvoo’s leadership seems to have vacillated over who was authorized to issue writs of habeas corpus under the ordinance. Section 1 of the 1827 Illinois statute on habeas corpus, upon which Nauvoo’s ordinance was based, limited the right to issue writs of habeas corpus to the state supreme court or the county circuit courts during their respective terms or to any of those courts’ judges individually during the courts’ vacations. Accordingly, early drafts of the city ordinance granted the power to the municipal court or any of its justices. However, perhaps recognizing the difficulty of appealing directly to the judges of the supreme and circuit courts, in 1835 the Illinois state legislature passed an act requiring the circuit court justices to appoint a master in chancery for each county who would then be authorized to issue certain procedural writs, such as those of habeas corpus. The final version of the Nauvoo ordinance similarly shifted the responsibility for issuing writs of habeas corpus from the justices to the clerk of the municipal court. (An Act Regulating the Proceeding on Writs of Habeas Corpus [22 Jan. 1827], Public and General Statute Laws of the State of Illinois, pp. 322–323, sec. 1; An Act to Provide for Issuing Writs of Ne Exeat and Habeas Corpus, and for Other Purposes [11 Feb. 1835], Public and General Statute Laws of the State of Illinois, p. 145, secs. 1–2.)
